In mathematical [[set theory]], the '''Laver property''' holds between two models if they are not "too dissimilar", in the following sense.

For <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> transitive models of set theory, <math>N</math> is said to have the Laver property over <math>M</math> if and only if for every function <math>g\in M</math> mapping <math>\omega</math> to <math>\omega\setminus\{0\}</math> such that <math>g</math> diverges to infinity, and every function <math>f\in N</math> mapping <math>\omega</math> to <math>\omega</math> and every function <math>h\in M</math> which bounds <math>f</math>, there is a tree <math>T\in M</math> such that each branch of <math>T</math> is bounded by <math>h</math> and for every <math>n</math> the <math>n^\text{th}</math> level of <math>T</math> has [[cardinality]] at most <math>g(n)</math> and <math>f</math> is a branch of <math>T</math>.<ref>Shelah, S., Consistently there is no non-trivial ccc forcing notion with the Sacks or Laver property, Combinatorica, vol. 2, pp. 309 -- 319, (2001)</ref>

A forcing notion is said to have the Laver property if and only if the forcing extension has the Laver property over the ground model.  Examples include [[List of forcing notions#Laver forcing|Laver forcing]].

The concept is named after [[Richard Laver]].

[[Saharon Shelah]] proved that when proper forcings with the Laver property are [[iterated forcing|iterated]] using countable supports, the resulting forcing notion will have the Laver property as well.<ref>Shelah, S., Proper and Improper Forcing, Springer (1992)</ref><ref>C. Schlindwein, Understanding preservation theorems: Chapter VI of Proper and Improper Forcing, I. Archive for Mathematical Logic, vol. 53, 171–202, Springer, 2014</ref>

The conjunction of the Laver property and the <math>{}^\omega\omega</math>-bounding property is equivalent to the [[Sacks property]].
